name: Troy (the mound of Hisarlik)
scope: A grassy mound called Hisarlik in northwest Turkey, the site of legendary Troy. T1: Hisarlik is not ONE Troy but at least nine cities stacked on top of each other over ~3,000 years, piling ~15 m of ruins into a single hill (each city built on the rubble of the last). T2: Homer's Iliad set the Trojan War at this place; the walls and towers are real, but the wooden-horse trick survives only as legend -- no horse was ever dug up. T3: in the 1870s Heinrich Schliemann used Homer as a treasure-map and drove a huge trench into the mound -- and his crude digging cut straight THROUGH the layer thought to be Homer's Troy, wrecking part of it. T4: the gold hoard he trumpeted as 'Priam's Treasure' came from the Troy II layer -- a city roughly 1,000 years too OLD to be King Priam's (the war-era city is Troy VI/VIIa, ~1250 BC). T5: at the Troy VIIa level archaeologists found a burn layer, scattered sling-stones and arrowheads, and bodies left unburied -- physical hints that a real city here was stormed and destroyed around the time of Homer's tale.
source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) checked first for Troy/Schliemann (blocked to automated fetch, 403); corroborated with well-established encyclopedic accounts (Wikipedia: Troy; Hisarlik; Heinrich Schliemann; Priam's Treasure). Layer dating (Troy I-IX, Troy VI/VIIa as candidate war city) and the Troy II misdating of 'Priam's Treasure' are standard archaeological consensus.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, lead with the scene (the layered hill), never 'Who found Troy?'. The accuracy rail is the LEGEND flag -- the wooden horse is myth (say so) and 'Priam's Treasure' is famously misdated (the treasure is real, the Priam label is wrong). Dinner-test payoff: the 'nine cities in one hill' rung and the 'treasure is 1,000 years too old' rung. Distractors stay live with other real Bronze-Age/archaeology facts, never the deduced answer. LANE: the Trojan War narrative and Schliemann's biography are the HISTORY bank's -- geography keeps the PLACE (the stratified mound, the destruction stratum, the walls).
history_overlap: The Trojan War as a Homeric/history episode and Heinrich Schliemann's biography likely appear in a history-bank ladder; keep geography anchored to the physical mound and its stacked cities, not the war narrative or Schliemann's life story.

name: Mycenae (the Lion Gate & the cyclopean walls)
scope: The hilltop citadel of Mycenae in the Greek Peloponnese, capital of Bronze-Age Greece. T1: over its main gate stand two carved stone lionesses flanking a column -- the Lion Gate, the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe still standing where it was built. T2: the fortress walls are made of blocks so gigantic that later Greeks refused to believe men had lifted them and said the one-eyed giant Cyclopes built them -- so we still call this 'cyclopean' masonry. T3: Schliemann dug up a golden death-mask in a grave here and cabled that he had 'gazed upon the face of Agamemnon' -- but the mask is about 300 years too old to be the Trojan-War king (a famous misattribution). T4: just outside stands the Treasury of Atreus, a beehive (tholos) tomb whose corbelled stone dome was the widest in the world for over 1,000 years -- until the Romans built the Pantheon. T5: clay tablets from Mycenaean palaces are written in Linear B, cracked in 1952 by Michael Ventris to reveal the OLDEST readable Greek -- Bronze-Age palace inventories.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Mycenae; Lion Gate; Treasury of Atreus (verified the corbelled-dome-largest-for-1,000-years-until-the-Pantheon claim and its ~1300-1250 BC date, 14.5 m diameter); Linear B / Michael Ventris (1952 decipherment).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led wonder. Accuracy rail: flag the 'Mask of Agamemnon' as a genuine MISATTRIBUTION (real gold mask, wrong king) and note 'cyclopean' is the Greeks' own legend-explanation for the huge stones. Dinner-test payoff: the cyclopean-walls rung and the Treasury of Atreus dome-record rung (it hands the baton to the Pantheon ladder). LANE: Agamemnon/the Trojan War and the Linear B decipherment story belong to history -- geography keeps the gate, the walls, and the tholos as place-wonder.
history_overlap: King Agamemnon / the Trojan War and the decipherment of Linear B may live in history-bank ladders; geography keeps the Lion Gate, cyclopean walls, and Treasury of Atreus as physical place-wonders.

name: Knossos (the Minoan palace & the Labyrinth)
scope: The great Bronze-Age palace of Knossos on Crete, heart of the Minoan civilization. T1: Knossos is a sprawling complex of some 1,300 interconnecting rooms, storerooms, and twisting corridors -- so maze-like that many think the real building inspired the myth of the Labyrinth. T2: that myth is anchored HERE: King Minos caged the bull-headed Minotaur in a labyrinth, and the hero Theseus escaped it by unspooling Ariadne's thread (legend tied to this place). T3: the palace's 'bull-leaping' fresco shows athletes vaulting over the horns of a charging bull -- a real Minoan ritual painted on these walls ~3,500 years ago. T4: Knossos had running water in clay pipes, stone drains, and what may be the oldest flushing toilet in Europe -- plumbing engineered ~3,700 years ago. T5: excavator Arthur Evans named the whole 'Minoan' civilization after King Minos and poured CONCRETE to 'restore' the palace in vivid reds and blues -- a reconstruction critics say is partly his own invention.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated with standard encyclopedic accounts (Wikipedia: Knossos; Minoan civilization; Arthur Evans; Bull-Leaping Fresco). The ~1,300-room count, the plumbing/early-flush-toilet claim, and Evans's concrete 'reconstitution' controversy are well-documented consensus.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the palace ITSELF is the wonder that may have birthed the labyrinth legend (so the myth rung is anchored to the real place, flagged as legend). Accuracy rail: label the Minotaur/Theseus story LEGEND, and present Evans's colorful reconstruction as CONTESTED (real palace, disputed restoration). Dinner-test payoff: the ~3,700-year-old flush toilet rung, and the labyrinth-inspired-by-the-real-maze rung. LANE: the Minoan civilization as a history topic and the Linear A/B scripts lean historical -- geography keeps the palace-as-place, the frescoes, and the plumbing.
history_overlap: The Minoan civilization and the Linear A/Linear B scripts may appear in history-bank ladders; geography keeps Knossos as a physical place (the maze-palace, frescoes, plumbing, Evans's reconstruction).

name: Akrotiri & the Thera eruption (Santorini)
scope: Santorini (ancient Thera) in the Aegean, and the Minoan-era town of Akrotiri buried under its volcano. T1: Santorini's dramatic curved bay is a caldera -- a giant drowned crater left when the island's volcano blew its top in the Bronze Age (teach: a caldera is the collapsed basin a volcano leaves after a huge eruption). T2: buried under the ash lies Akrotiri, a Minoan-era town preserved like Pompeii -- but about 1,600 years EARLIER, with two- and three-story houses still standing to their upper floors. T3: unlike Pompeii, almost NO bodies and barely any treasure were found -- the townspeople seem to have felt the warning earthquakes and evacuated in good order before the blast. T4: the ash sealed brilliant wall-paintings -- the 'Spring Fresco' of swallows darting over red lilies -- and preserved hollow molds of vanished wooden furniture. T5: because a whole advanced island civilization here was swallowed by the sea and ash, some scholars have linked Thera to Plato's story of Atlantis -- a real but SPECULATIVE hypothesis, not proven.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Akrotiri (prehistoric city) -- verified Minoan links (Linear A, fresco style), no uninterred human remains (orderly evacuation), Spring Fresco (found 1970), Marinatos excavation from 1967, eruption dated 16th century BC (~1620-1530 BCE). The Atlantis link is a real scholarly hypothesis but explicitly speculative.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led wonder (the caldera bay, then the buried town). Accuracy rail: the caldera term is taught before it's tested, AND the Atlantis connection is clearly flagged as a SPECULATIVE hypothesis, never stated as fact. Dinner-test payoff: the evacuated town where almost no bodies were found -- the eerie contrast with Pompeii. LANE: the caldera as a landform overlaps the earthsystem/volcanism strand -- here the ANCHOR is the buried Minoan town, not the eruption mechanics; the Minoan collapse leans historical, so keep the payoff the PLACE.
history_overlap: The Minoan collapse / Bronze-Age Aegean history may appear in history; the volcanic caldera mechanics overlap the geography earthsystem-volcanism strand -- keep this ladder anchored to the buried town of Akrotiri and its preservation.

name: Delphi (the oracle at the navel of the world)
scope: The sanctuary of Delphi on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in Greece. T1: the ancient Greeks marked Delphi as the omphalos, the 'navel of the world' -- the exact center of the earth -- and a carved dome-shaped stone stood here to prove it (teach: omphalos means navel). T2: WHY the center? Legend says Zeus released two eagles from opposite edges of the world and they met right HERE, so this spot was named the middle of everything. T3: kings and generals journeyed to Delphi to ask the oracle -- a priestess called the Pythia -- for prophecies, often maddeningly riddling (Croesus was told 'a great empire will fall' if he attacked Persia; the empire that fell was his own). T4: the Pythia gave her prophecies over a crack in the temple floor; geologists have since found fault lines beneath Delphi that may once have released mind-altering gases -- a debated modern theory. T5: carved on Apollo's temple were the words 'Know thyself' (gnothi seauton) -- a place where prophecy and philosophy met.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated with standard classical references (Wikipedia: Delphi; Pythia; Omphalos; Oracle of Delphi). The geological-gas hypothesis (fault lines / ethylene) is a real but debated modern theory (de Boer et al.) and is flagged as such.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER (the sanctuary and its 'center of the world' claim). Accuracy rail: the intoxicating-vapors idea is a DEBATED modern theory (flag it), and the Croesus prophecy is a famous historical anecdote (attribute it, don't invent a quote). Dinner-test payoff: the two eagles meeting at the omphalos. LANE: the oracle's political role across Greek history leans historical, and 'Know thyself' brushes the philosophy bank -- geography keeps the PLACE (the omphalos, the sanctuary, the geology).
history_overlap: The oracle's influence on Greek political history and the 'Know thyself' maxim may surface in history/philosophy ladders; geography keeps Delphi as a place -- the omphalos, the sanctuary on Parnassus, and the fault-line geology.

name: Pompeii & Herculaneum (frozen by Vesuvius, AD 79)
scope: Two Roman towns near Naples buried by Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. T1: when Vesuvius erupted, ash and hot flows buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in hours, sealing the towns to lie forgotten for about 1,700 years. T2: the ash hardened around victims who then decayed, leaving body-shaped hollows -- so archaeologists poured plaster into the voids to cast the people in their final poses (the plaster-cast technique). T3: Pompeii's walls still carry Roman graffiti -- election slogans, insults, and a doorway mosaic reading 'CAVE CANEM' ('Beware of Dog') -- everyday life frozen mid-sentence. T4: Herculaneum, buried deeper under hotter flows, was CARBONIZED (turned to charcoal rather than crushed), preserving a library of roughly 1,800 papyrus scrolls at the Villa of the Papyri. T5: those scrolls are too fragile to unroll -- so the Vesuvius Challenge used X-ray scans and AI to read them VIRTUALLY, recovering lost words of the philosopher Philodemus without ever opening them.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Herculaneum papyri (verified ~1,800 scrolls at the Villa of the Papyri; Vesuvius Challenge -- 'porphyras' Oct 2023, $700k grand prize Feb 2024, first full virtual unwrapping of PHerc. 1667 in 2026; Philodemus texts). Pompeii plaster casts (Fiorelli method) and the AD 79 eruption are standard consensus.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, drama in the STEM (the buried towns). Accuracy rail: keep the preservation SCIENCE exact -- Herculaneum was carbonized (not simply crushed), and the scroll-reading is genuinely recent (2023-2026), so state it as the current breakthrough it is. Dinner-test payoff: the AI-read carbonized scrolls (a lost philosopher recovered without unrolling) -- and the plaster body-casts. LANE: the eruption's volcanic mechanics belong to the earthsystem-volcanism strand and Pliny the Younger's eyewitness letter leans historical -- keep the anchor the PLACES and their frozen-in-time preservation.
history_overlap: The AD 79 eruption as an event and Pliny the Younger's eyewitness account may appear in history; Vesuvius's eruption mechanics overlap the earthsystem-volcanism strand. Keep this ladder on the towns' preservation (casts, graffiti, carbonized scrolls).

name: The Colosseum (Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre)
scope: The Colosseum in Rome, the giant Flavian Amphitheatre (completed ~AD 80). T1: the Colosseum could seat around 50,000 spectators, funneled through 80 arched entrances so a packed crowd could pour out in minutes. T2: a vast retractable awning, the velarium, shaded the seats -- rigged and hauled overhead by sailors from the Roman navy, who alone knew how to work the ropes and rigging. T3: beneath the arena floor lay the hypogeum, a two-level maze of tunnels with lift-and-pulley elevators and trap doors that made animals and scenery appear as if by magic. T4: the very earliest games may have FLOODED the arena for mock sea-battles (naumachiae) -- but once the hypogeum was dug out beneath the floor, flooding became impossible, so scholars still debate how it was ever done (flag: disputed). T5: the stone is pocked all over with holes where iron clamps once bound the travertine blocks together -- later scavengers pried the metal out to melt down.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Colosseum -- verified capacity ~50,000; velarium worked by sailors from Misenum; hypogeum elevators/pulleys; and that the naumachia flooding is DEBATED and ended once the hypogeum was built under Domitian.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, engineering as the marvel. Accuracy rail: the naumachia (flooded sea-battle) rung MUST be framed as DISPUTED -- ancient sources describe early water spectacles, but the hypogeum made later flooding impossible, so present it as a genuine open question, not settled fact. Teach velarium and hypogeum before testing them. Dinner-test payoff: the flooded arena for mock sea-battles, plus the hypogeum's trap-door elevators. LANE: gladiatorial games as Roman social history lean historical -- geography keeps the PLACE (velarium, hypogeum, travertine engineering).
history_overlap: Gladiatorial games / Roman spectacle as a social-history topic may appear in history; keep this ladder on the building's engineering (seating flow, velarium, hypogeum, travertine construction).

name: The Pantheon (Rome's unbeaten concrete dome)
scope: The Pantheon in Rome, a temple rebuilt under Hadrian (~AD 118-128). T1: nearly 1,900 years on, the Pantheon still wears the largest UNREINFORCED concrete dome on Earth -- no modern concrete dome built without steel has ever surpassed it. T2: the dome is a perfect half-sphere -- its height equals its interior width (43.3 m) -- so a full 43-meter ball would fit exactly inside. T3: at the very top gapes the oculus, a ~9-meter hole open to the open sky; rain really does fall through it and drains away through slanted holes in the sloped marble floor (teach: oculus means 'eye'). T4: the Romans made the concrete LIGHTER toward the top -- heavy travertine chips near the base, light volcanic pumice near the oculus -- so the dome would not crush itself under its own weight. T5: almost every other ancient Roman temple was quarried away for its stone -- the Pantheon survived nearly intact because in AD 609 it was converted into a Christian church.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Pantheon, Rome -- verified 'still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome'; 43.3 m equal height/diameter with a fitting sphere; oculus with sloped drained floor; lightweight-aggregate gradient (travertine to tufa/pumice); Hadrian rebuild with the Agrippa inscription; survival via conversion to a church in 609.
framing_note: Voice: INVERT THE WONDER -- put the record (biggest unreinforced concrete dome, still) in the stem as the hook. Accuracy rail: keep it precise to 'unreinforced concrete dome' (not all domes), and teach 'oculus' before testing it. Dinner-test payoff: rain actually falling through the open oculus, and the still-champion concrete dome. LANE: the Hadrian/Agrippa attribution is a mild history point -- geography keeps the PLACE and its engineering. Note a light cross-link: the Rome city-ladder samples the Pantheon's oculus among several Rome wonders; this ladder deep-dives the single monument.
history_overlap: The Hadrian-rebuilt / Agrippa-inscription attribution is a minor history point; keep the ladder on the building's engineering (the concrete dome, oculus, weight gradient, its survival).

name: Stonehenge (Salisbury Plain)
scope: The great stone ring of Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain, England. T1: the biggest 'sarsen' stones stand in a ring capped by level lintels locked on with mortise-and-tenon joints -- carpentry joinery worked in solid stone ~4,500 years ago. T2: at midsummer sunrise the sun climbs directly over the outlying Heel Stone and along the monument's axis -- Stonehenge works as a ~5,000-year-old solar calendar (teach the solstice alignment through the scene). T3: the smaller 'bluestones' were hauled about 230 km from the Preseli Hills of WALES -- among the longest-distance monument-stone transports of the ancient world. T4: the huge sarsens, by contrast, came from West Woods near Marlborough, only ~25 km away -- pinned to that exact source in 2020 by matching their chemical fingerprint. T5: the flat 'Altar Stone,' long grouped with the Welsh bluestones, was traced in 2024 to NORTHEAST SCOTLAND -- over 700 km away -- a discovery that rewrote how far Neolithic Britons moved stone.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Altar Stone (Stonehenge) -- verified the 2024 finding that the Altar Stone came from the Orcadian Basin in NE Scotland. Bluestones from the Preseli Hills (Wales, ~230 km) and sarsens traced to West Woods near Marlborough in a 2020 study (Nash et al.) are standard consensus; mortise-and-tenon lintel joints and the Heel Stone midsummer alignment likewise.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led wonder (the stones and their alignment), never 'What is Stonehenge?'. Accuracy rail: the three stone SOURCES must be kept exactly distinct -- bluestones (Wales), sarsens (Marlborough, 2020), Altar Stone (NE Scotland, 2024) -- so distractors are the OTHER real sources, all live. Dinner-test payoff: the Altar Stone traced to Scotland (a fresh 2024 shock) and the Welsh bluestones. LANE: purely prehistoric, no written-history overlap.

name: Newgrange & Bru na Boinne (the solstice tomb)
scope: Newgrange, a great passage-tomb in Ireland's Boyne Valley. T1: Newgrange is a huge grass-topped mound of stone built around 3200 BC -- OLDER than Stonehenge and older than the Great Pyramid of Giza. T2: above the entrance is a stone 'roof-box'; for a few mornings around the winter solstice the rising sun shoots a beam down a 19-meter passage to flood the inner chamber with light for about 17 minutes. T3: the great entrance stone is carved with a triple spiral (triskele) -- a 5,000-year-old design cut with nothing but stone tools. T4: the chamber's corbelled roof -- overlapping flat stones with no mortar (teach: corbelling) -- has kept the inner room bone-DRY for over 5,000 years. T5: Newgrange is one of three giant tombs, with Knowth and Dowth, in Bru na Boinne -- a whole Neolithic ritual landscape older than the pharaohs.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Newgrange -- verified ~3200/3100 BC (older than Stonehenge and Giza), the roof-box winter-solstice beam lighting the chamber ~17 minutes (O'Kelly's 1967 observation), the triple-spiral entrance stone, the still-dry corbelled vault, and its place within Bru na Boinne (Knowth, Dowth).
framing_note: Voice: INVERT THE WONDER -- open with 'older than the pyramids' as the hook and let 'Newgrange' / the specific feature be the answer. Accuracy rail: the age comparison is exact (~3200 BC, before Giza and Stonehenge's stones); teach 'corbelled' before testing it. Dinner-test payoff: the winter-solstice sunbeam threading 19 m of passage, and the older-than-the-pyramids age. LANE: prehistoric -- no written-history overlap.

name: Carnac (the Breton stone alignments)
scope: The Carnac stones in Brittany, France -- the world's greatest field of standing stones. T1: near Carnac, more than 3,000 standing stones (menhirs) march in long parallel rows across the fields -- the largest alignment of standing stones on Earth (teach: a menhir is a single upright standing stone). T2: they are OLDER than Stonehenge and the pyramids -- raised roughly 4500-3300 BC by some of Europe's earliest farmers. T3: nobody is sure WHY they stand in rows -- astronomy, ceremonial processions, territory markers? -- the purpose is genuinely debated and unknown (flag it). T4: nearby at Locmariaquer once stood the Grand Menhir Brise, the biggest single standing stone ever raised (~20 m tall) -- now toppled and broken into four huge pieces. T5: a local Christian legend says St Cornelius turned an entire Roman army to stone here, which is why the stones stand in ranks -- a folk tale, not history (flag as legend).
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated with standard references (Wikipedia: Carnac stones; Grand Menhir Brise). The >3,000-menhir count, the ~4500-3300 BC dating (predating Stonehenge), the debated purpose, and the Grand Menhir Brise (~20 m, fallen in four pieces) are consensus; the St Cornelius tale is well-known folklore.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led wonder (thousands of stones in ranks). Accuracy rail: the PURPOSE is honestly flagged as unknown/debated, and the St Cornelius story is labeled LEGEND. Dinner-test payoff: the 3,000+ stones marching in rows, and the giant broken Grand Menhir. LANE: prehistoric -- no written-history overlap. Teach 'menhir' before testing it.

name: The Ice-Age painted caves (Lascaux, Chauvet, Altamira)
scope: Europe's great Ice-Age painted caves. T1: deep inside Lascaux cave in France, Ice-Age artists painted a 'Hall of the Bulls' -- huge galloping animals in ochre and charcoal about 17,000 years ago. T2: Lascaux was found in 1940 by four teenagers whose dog disappeared down a hole; within years visitors' breath grew mold on the art and it was SEALED -- today you tour an exact replica (Lascaux II/IV), not the real cave. T3: France's Chauvet Cave holds some of the OLDEST paintings known -- lions, rhinos, and horses roughly 36,500 years old -- and it too is sealed shut, copied as the 'Caverne du Pont-d'Arc.' T4: at Altamira in Spain, the bison ceiling was so vivid that when a girl and her father reported it in 1879, experts wrongly cried FORGERY -- no one believed cave-people could paint that well. T5: these painters used the cave's own bulges and hollows as the animals' muscles, blew powdered pigment through tubes to spray outlines, and pressed hand stencils -- a shared Ice-Age technique across Europe.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Chauvet Cave -- verified ~36,500-year paintings ('some of the oldest known,' not definitively the world's oldest), discovery Dec 1994, sealed to the public, and the Caverne du Pont-d'Arc replica (2015). Lascaux (1940 discovery by teenagers, closed 1963, replicas) and Altamira (1879, initially dismissed as forgery) are standard consensus.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; each rung names a concrete cave. Accuracy rail: Chauvet is 'AMONG the oldest known' cave art -- do NOT call it the oldest in the world (older figurative art is now known outside Europe), and the closed-caves-toured-as-replicas fact must be exact. Dinner-test payoff: the dog-found Lascaux, and the 1879 'forgery' blunder at Altamira. LANE: the caves DEPICT animals, but the wonder is the ART and the PLACE -- keep answers about the paintings/caves, never a painted creature's biology (that would be the animal bank).

name: Skara Brae & Neolithic Orkney
scope: Skara Brae, a Stone-Age village on Orkney off northern Scotland. T1: in 1850 a fierce storm stripped away the coastal dunes at the Bay of Skaill and laid bare Skara Brae -- a stone village that had lain hidden for about 5,000 years. T2: it is OLDER than Stonehenge and the pyramids (~3200-2500 BC) and so well preserved it is nicknamed the 'Scottish Pompeii.' T3: because Orkney had almost no trees, the villagers built their FURNITURE from stone -- beds, seats, and dressers still stand inside the houses. T4: the homes are linked by low covered passages and even had built-in drains, with a small stone 'toilet' cubicle plumbed into each house. T5: Skara Brae sits in a wider Neolithic complex -- the Ring of Brodgar stone circle and the great Ness of Brodgar temple site -- a ritual heartland at Europe's northern edge.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated with standard references (Wikipedia: Skara Brae; Heart of Neolithic Orkney; Ness of Brodgar). The 1850-storm exposure, ~3200-2500 BC dating (older than Stonehenge/Giza), the stone furniture, the drains/toilets, and the wider Brodgar complex are consensus.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led wonder (a storm uncovers a lost village). Accuracy rail: the 'Scottish Pompeii' is a NICKNAME (a preservation comparison, not a claim it was volcano-buried) -- keep that clear. Dinner-test payoff: the storm-revealed village and its 5,000-year-old STONE furniture (beds and dressers). LANE: prehistoric -- no written-history overlap.

name: Ggantija & Malta's megalithic temples
scope: The megalithic temples of Malta, some of the oldest free-standing buildings on Earth. T1: on the small island of Gozo, the Ggantija temples were raised around 3600 BC -- among the world's oldest FREE-STANDING stone structures, older than the pyramids and Stonehenge. T2: some blocks weigh over 50 tons, so massive that Maltese legend says a giantess named Sansuna carried them -- 'Ggantija' means 'of the giants.' T3: builders with no metal tools and no wheels may have rolled the megaliths on small stone spheres used like ball-bearings -- some of these have actually been found at the sites. T4: cut into the rock nearby, the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum is an underground temple of the dead carved DOWNWARD through three levels -- with a chamber, the 'Oracle Room,' that resonates a deep hum when a voice speaks into it. T5: at the temple of Mnajdra the doorway is aligned so the EQUINOX sunrise shines straight down the central axis -- a Stone-Age solar clock on the Mediterranean.
source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Ggantija -- verified ~3600 BC ('over 5,500 years old,' among the oldest free-standing religious structures, older than pyramids and Stonehenge), the 'place of giants' / giantess Sansuna legend, the stone-sphere 'ball-bearing' transport, the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum, and Mnajdra's equinox-sunrise alignment.
framing_note: Voice: INVERT THE WONDER -- open with the age/size (older than the pyramids, 50-ton blocks) and make the named place/feature the answer. Accuracy rail: the giantess story is labeled LEGEND (it only explains the name), while the ball-bearing spheres and the equinox alignment are real archaeology. Dinner-test payoff: the stone 'ball-bearings,' and the humming 'Oracle Room' of the Hypogeum. LANE: teach 'megalith'/'hypogeum'; purely prehistoric, no written-history overlap.
